extracted_claims.text: Providers of general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act must draw up and maintain technical documentation, including training/testing processes and evaluation results, and provide it to the AI Office and national competent authorities upon request.
Providers of general-purpose AI models must make certain information and documentation available to downstream providers who intend to integrate the model into their own AI systems.
Providers of general-purpose AI models must put in place a copyright policy and publish a sufficiently detailed public summary of the content used for training.
Open-source general-purpose AI models are exempt from some documentation requirements under Article 53, unless classified as general-purpose AI models with systemic risk.
General-purpose AI models can be classified as having 'systemic risk' under Article 51, triggering additional obligations under Article 55 beyond the baseline Article 53 obligations.
Article 101 of the AI Act establishes a framework of fines applicable to providers of general-purpose AI models.
The EU AI Act is described as the world's first comprehensive horizontal legal framework for AI, regulating AI systems via a risk-based approach including specific rules for foundation models.

In the United States, there is currently no directly comparable single, economy-wide federal AI law with a horizontal structure comparable to the EU AI Act; the US compliance environment is described as more sector- or state-specific.

In late 2025, President Trump issued an executive order, 'Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence,' directing creation of a single, minimally burdensome national AI framework and seeking to pre-empt conflicting state AI laws.
The executive order directed preparation of a legislative proposal to Congress for a uniform federal AI framework.

On March 20, 2026, the White House released a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence urging Congress to replace the state-law patchwork with a uniform federal approach; the framework is non-binding and creates no immediate compliance obligations, and existing state AI laws remain operative unless Congress legislates.

The March 2026 National Policy Framework set in motion a DOJ litigation effort to contest certain state AI laws, a Commerce Department evaluation of burdensome state laws, and an FTC policy position on applying consumer-protection law to AI, and signaled possible conditioning of federal funding.
On the same day the National Policy Framework was released (per source 20), Democratic legislators introduced the GUARDRAILS Act as a competing legislative proposal.

On June 2, 2026, President Trump signed Executive Order 14409, 'Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security,' directing agencies to harden federal infrastructure against AI risks and establishing a voluntary framework for secure deployment of frontier AI models, including a 'covered frontier model' designation.
EO 14409's voluntary frontier model security framework contrasts with the EU AI Act's mandatory, binding obligations for general-purpose AI model providers.

The US previously relied on non-binding frameworks such as the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, which set out broad principles but were not enforceable, unlike the EU AI Act's binding requirements.

The US approach to AI governance has been characterized as permissive and focused on innovation, decentralized self-regulation, and reliance on existing laws, in contrast to the EU's prevention-based, prohibition-unless-permitted risk model with centralized regulation and specific penalties.

US AI policy has been characterized as subject to reactive deregulation and instability across administrations, exemplified by rescission of Biden Executive Order 14110, contrasting with the EU's more stable legislative approach.
The EU AI Act is framed as adaptive, rights-based legislation intended to remain interoperable with global frameworks, in contrast to current US and Chinese regulatory models.

The US AI.gov Action Plan emphasizes innovation, market forces, private sector leadership, and national security, relying on existing laws and executive guidance rather than detailed bans, in contrast to the EU AI Act's strict, binding rules prioritizing fundamental rights.

As of 2023, the EU AI Act had taken a legislative, categorization-based approach with specific reporting and oversight requirements, while the US SAFE Innovation Framework was a non-binding suggested framework emphasizing bipartisanship.
The US has not yet enacted durable, bipartisan federal AI legislation; commentary argues the US must move beyond executive orders to establish stable guardrails and enforcement mechanisms.

The EU AI Act addresses foundation model safety rules, transparency, accountability of developers, high-risk application definitions, prohibited applications, and implementation/enforcement mechanisms as part of a comprehensive framework.

report:
# EU AI Act Foundation Model Requirements vs. US Federal AI Policy: A Comparative Report

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act imposes binding, detailed obligations on providers of general-purpose AI models, backed by fines, while the United States continues to lack a comparable horizontal federal statute, relying instead on a shifting mix of executive orders, voluntary frameworks, and proposed legislation. This divergence reflects a broader pattern: the EU's prevention-based, rights-centered regulatory model contrasts with the US's innovation-focused, largely non-binding approach, though recent 2025–2026 US executive actions signal movement toward a more centralized (if still non-binding) federal posture.

## Key Findings

### EU AI Act Obligations for Foundation Model Providers
Providers of general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act must create and maintain technical documentation—covering training/testing processes and evaluation results—and make it available to the AI Office and national authorities on request (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53), [EU AI Act](https://www.euaiact.com/article/53)). They must also share specified information with downstream providers integrating the model into their own systems (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53)). Additional obligations include maintaining a copyright policy and publishing a detailed public summary of training content (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53)). Open-source models receive partial exemptions from these documentation duties unless classified as posing "systemic risk" (medium confidence), a classification under Article 51 that triggers added obligations under Article 55 (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53), [AI Act Explorer](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act-explorer)). Non-compliance can trigger fines under Article 101 (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-101)). The Act is widely characterized as the world's first comprehensive, horizontal legal framework for AI, combining risk-based categorization with specific foundation model rules (high confidence) ([EEAS](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/delegations/united-states-america/brussels-bay-eu-ai-act_en)).

### US Federal Approach: Absence of a Comparable Law
The US currently has no single, economy-wide federal AI law structurally comparable to the EU AI Act; its compliance landscape is described as sector- and state-specific (medium confidence) ([European Court of Auditors](https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAPublications/JOURNAL-2026-01/JOURNAL-2026-01_EN.pdf)). Earlier US efforts, such as the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, offered non-binding principles rather than enforceable rules (medium confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/de/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/practical-organizational-framework-ai-accountability)).

### Recent US Executive Actions (2025–2026)
In late 2025, an executive order, "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence," directed creation of a unified, minimally burdensome federal approach and sought to preempt conflicting state AI laws (medium confidence), including directing a legislative proposal to Congress (medium confidence) ([European Parliament](https://espas.secure.europarl.europa.eu/orbis/system/files/generated/document/en/Near-term-Future-Transatlantic-Relationship-FINAL.pdf)). A related White House National Policy Framework reportedly released in March 2026 urged Congress to replace the state patchwork with a uniform approach, though it remains non-binding with no immediate compliance obligations (low confidence) ([Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CSA_research_note_whitehouse-national-ai-policy-framework-enterprise-security_20260411-csa-styled.pdf)). This framework reportedly spurred a DOJ litigation effort against state AI laws, a Commerce Department review, and FTC consumer-protection activity (low confidence) ([Collibra](https://www.collibra.com/blog/ai-regulatory-compliance-in-2026-eu-ai-act-us-orders-and-state-laws-and-how-to-operationalize)). Separately, on June 2, 2026, Executive Order 14409 established a voluntary framework for securing "covered frontier models" and hardening federal infrastructure (medium confidence) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_of_artificial_intelligence_in_the_United_States), [Congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/HTML/IF13268.html)). This voluntary structure stands in clear contrast to the EU's mandatory, binding GPAI requirements (high confidence) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_of_artificial_intelligence_in_the_United_States), [European Court of Auditors](https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAPublications/JOURNAL-2026-01/JOURNAL-2026-01_EN.pdf)).

### Broader Interpretive Comparisons
Analysts characterize the US approach as permissive, innovation-focused, and reliant on existing laws and self-regulation, versus the EU's prohibition-unless-permitted, centralized risk model (low confidence) ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21279v1)). US policy has also been described as unstable across administrations, exemplified by the rescission of Executive Order 14110 (low confidence) ([DCN Global](https://dcnglobal.net/posts/blog/us-vs-eu-ai-plans-a-comparative-analysis-of-the-us-and-european-approaches)). The EU AI Act is framed as adaptive, rights-based legislation intended for global interoperability (medium confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/778575/ECTI_STU(2025)778575_EN.pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on the precise origin and timeline of the key US federal pivot: one describes a "late 2025" executive order, while another references distinct December 2025 and March 2026 instruments, creating ambiguity about sequencing and naming ([European Parliament](https://espas.secure.europarl.europa.eu/orbis/system/files/generated/document/en/Near-term-Future-Transatlantic-Relationship-FINAL.pdf), [Collibra](https://www.collibra.com/blog/ai-regulatory-compliance-in-2026-eu-ai-act-us-orders-and-state-laws-and-how-to-operationalize)). Several claims regarding the March 2026 Framework, the GUARDRAILS Act, and related enforcement actions carry low confidence (below 0.4) and should be treated cautiously pending verification.

## Knowledge Gaps
Key unresolved questions include: whether EU Article 101 fines have been applied in practice to GPAI providers; whether the US legislative proposal has been introduced in Congress and what it would require; the fate of the GUARDRAILS Act; how EO 14409's voluntary framework might evolve toward binding rules; the outcome of DOJ litigation against state AI laws; and whether the US will ultimately adopt any horizontal AI statute comparable to the EU AI Act.
